children.name: Macropus
children.description: The 'true' kangaroos in the strict modern sense — after extensive reclassification, this genus now contains only the two grey kangaroos. Both are grazers of open woodland and grassland and are among the most recognisable marsupials on Earth, with eastern and western species together numbering in the tens of millions.

children.name: Macropus giganteus
children.description: The eastern grey kangaroo (Macropus giganteus: gigantic large-foot; also great grey kangaroo or forester kangaroo) is a marsupial found in the eastern third of Australia, with a population of several million.

children.name: Macropus fuliginosus
children.description: The western grey kangaroo (Macropus fuliginosus), also referred to as a western grey giant kangaroo, black-faced kangaroo, mallee kangaroo, sooty kangaroo and (when referring to the Kangaroo Island subspecies) Kangaroo Island grey kangaroo, is a large and very common kangaroo found across almost the entire southern part of Australia, from just south of Shark Bay through coastal Western Australia and South Australia, into western Victoria, and in the entire Murray–Darling basin in New South Wales and Queensland.

children.name: Osphranter
children.description: The wallaroos and the Red Kangaroo — the largest living marsupial. Osphranter was long lumped inside Macropus but reinstated as a distinct genus after molecular studies confirmed deep divergence. The Red Kangaroo is an icon of the arid interior; the wallaroos occupy rocky ranges and cliffs from the tropics to the south.

children.name: Osphranter rufus
children.description: The red kangaroo (Osphranter rufus ) is the largest of all kangaroos, the largest terrestrial mammal native to Australia, and the largest extant marsupial.

children.name: Osphranter antilopinus
children.description: The antilopine kangaroo (Osphranter antilopinus), also known as the antilopine wallaroo or the antilopine wallaby, is a species of macropod found in northern Australia: in Cape York Peninsula in Queensland, the Top End of the Northern Territory, and the Kimberley region of Western Australia.

children.name: Osphranter robustus
children.description: The common wallaroo (Osphranter robustus), also known as the euro, hill wallaroo, or simply wallaroo,.

children.name: Osphranter bernardus
children.description: The black wallaroo (Osphranter bernardus), also known as Woodward's wallaroo, is a species of macropod restricted to a small, mountainous area in Arnhem Land, Northern Territory, Australia, between South Alligator River and Nabarlek.

children.name: Notamacropus
children.description: The scrub wallabies — a diverse assemblage of medium-sized macropods distributed from coastal heathlands to tropical savannas. Previously buried inside the sprawling genus Macropus, molecular work elevated Notamacropus to full generic rank in 2019. Many are among Australia's most familiar wildlife but several island and coastal species face significant pressure.

children.name: Notamacropus agilis
children.description: The agile wallaby (Notamacropus agilis), also known as the sandy wallaby, is a species of wallaby found in northern Australia and southern New Guinea.

children.name: Notamacropus rufogriseus
children.description: The red-necked wallaby or Bennett's wallaby is a medium-sized macropod marsupial (wallaby), common in the more temperate and fertile parts of eastern Australia, including Tasmania. Red-necked wallabies have been introduced to several other countries, including New Zealand, the United Kingdom, Ireland, the Isle of Man, France and Germany.

children.name: Notamacropus eugenii
children.description: The tammar wallaby (Notamacropus eugenii), also known as the dama wallaby or darma wallaby, is a small macropod native to South and Western Australia.

children.name: Notamacropus parma
children.description: The parma wallaby (Notamacropus parma) is a small marsupial macropod mammal native to forests and densely-vegetated areas of northeastern New South Wales, Australia, close to the border with Queensland.

children.name: Notamacropus parryi
children.description: The whiptail wallaby (Notamacropus parryi), also known as the pretty-faced wallaby, is a species of wallaby found in eastern Australia.

children.name: Notamacropus dorsalis
children.description: The black-striped wallaby (Notamacropus dorsalis), also known as the scrub wallaby or eastern brush wallaby, is a medium-sized wallaby found in Australia, from Townsville in Queensland to Narrabri in New South Wales..

children.name: Wallabia
children.description: A monotypic genus containing the Swamp Wallaby — the most genetically distinct of all macropods. Unlike every other member of the family, it does not share the standard macropod chromosome number, a distinction so dramatic that it cannot hybridise with any close relative. It has also been observed to begin a second pregnancy while still gestating the first.

children.name: Wallabia bicolor
children.description: The swamp wallaby (Wallabia bicolor) is a small macropod marsupial of eastern Australia.

children.name: Setonix
children.description: A monotypic genus and one of the smallest macropods. Setonix is most closely related to the pademelons (Thylogale) and shares with them a compact, stocky build suited to dense vegetation. Today it is essentially restricted to two small islands off Western Australia — Rottnest Island and Bald Island — though it once ranged across the mainland's south-west.

children.name: Setonix brachyurus
children.description: The quokka (; Setonix brachyurus) is a small macropod about the size of a domestic cat..

children.name: Onychogalea
children.description: The nailtail wallabies, named for a small horny spur at the tip of their tail whose function remains unknown. All three species were once widespread across Australia's interior grasslands; one — the crescent nailtail wallaby — is extinct, and the bridled nailtail wallaby is critically endangered, with fewer than 500 individuals surviving in central Queensland.

children.name: Onychogalea fraenata
children.description: The bridled nail-tail wallaby (Onychogalea fraenata), also known as the bridled nail-tailed wallaby, bridled nailtail wallaby, bridled wallaby, merrin, and flashjack, is a vulnerable species of macropod.

children.name: Onychogalea unguifera
children.description: The northern or sandy nail-tail wallaby (Onychogalea unguifera) is a species of macropod found across northern Australia on arid and sparsely wooded plains..

children.name: Onychogalea lunata
children.description: The crescent nail-tail wallaby, also known as the worong (Onychogalea lunata), is a small species of marsupial that grazed on grasses in the scrub and woodlands of southwestern and central Australia.

children.name: Thylogale
children.description: The pademelons — compact, short-tailed macropods of forest edges and dense vegetation from eastern Australia through New Guinea. They bound on all four limbs through thick undergrowth rather than hopping on two, and their cryptic brown coats make them difficult to spot in the dim light of forest floors.

children.name: Thylogale thetis
children.description: The red-necked pademelon (Thylogale thetis) is a forest-dwelling marsupial living in the eastern coastal region of Australia between extreme south-east Queensland and central eastern New South Wales..

children.name: Thylogale stigmatica
children.description: The red-legged pademelon (Thylogale stigmatica) is a species of small macropod found on the northeastern coast of Australia and in New Guinea..

children.name: Thylogale billardierii
children.description: The Tasmanian pademelon (Thylogale billardierii), also known as the rufous-bellied pademelon or red-bellied pademelon, is the sole species of pademelon found in Tasmania, and was formerly found throughout southeastern Australia.

children.name: Thylogale brunii
children.description: The dusky pademelon or dusky wallaby (Thylogale brunii) is a species of marsupial in the family Macropodidae.

children.name: Petrogale
children.description: The rock-wallabies — a spectacular radiation of 16 species that have evolved to navigate cliff faces and rocky outcrops with remarkable agility. Their feet have granulated, friction-pad soles and stiff hind claws that grip rough surfaces. Many species are now isolated on 'habitat islands' — isolated rock formations in an otherwise inhospitable landscape — and several are endangered.

children.name: Petrogale xanthopus
children.description: The yellow-footed rock-wallaby (Petrogale xanthopus), formerly known as the ring-tailed rock-wallaby, is a member of the macropod family (the marsupial family that includes the kangaroos, wallabies, tree-kangaroos, and wallaroos)..

children.name: Petrogale penicillata
children.description: The brush-tailed rock-wallaby or small-eared rock-wallaby (Petrogale penicillata) is a kind of wallaby, one of several rock-wallabies in the genus Petrogale..

children.name: Petrogale lateralis
children.description: The black-flanked rock-wallaby (Petrogale lateralis), also known as the black-footed rock-wallaby or warru, is a species of wallaby, one of several rock-wallabies in the genus Petrogale..

children.name: Petrogale brachyotis
children.description: The short-eared rock-wallaby (Petrogale brachyotis) is a species of rock-wallaby found in northern Australia, in the northernmost parts of the Northern Territory and Western Australia..

children.name: Petrogale concinna
children.description: The nabarlek (Petrogale concinna) is a small species of macropod found in northern Australia..

children.name: Dendrolagus
children.description: The tree-kangaroos — an extraordinary reversal of the macropod body plan back to an arboreal life. Their ancestors were ground-dwelling hoppers; over millions of years the tree-kangaroos evolved stronger forelimbs, shorter and broader hind feet, and a long tail for balance as they returned to the canopy. Most species live in the rainforests of New Guinea; two are native to northern Queensland.

children.name: Dendrolagus lumholtzi
children.description: Lumholtz's tree-kangaroo (Dendrolagus lumholtzi) is a arboreal, long-tailed marsupial found in rainforests in northeastern Australia..

children.name: Dendrolagus bennettianus
children.description: Bennett's tree-kangaroo (Dendrolagus bennettianus) is a large tree-kangaroo..

children.name: Dendrolagus goodfellowi
children.description: Goodfellow's tree-kangaroo (Dendrolagus goodfellowi), also called the ornate tree-kangaroo, is an endangered, long-tailed mammal native to rainforests of New Guinea..

children.name: Dendrolagus matschiei
children.description: Matschie's tree-kangaroo (Dendrolagus matschiei), also known as the Huon tree-kangaroo is a tree-kangaroo native to the Huon Peninsula of northeastern New Guinea island, within the nation of Papua New Guinea..

children.name: Dendrolagus dorianus
children.description: Doria's tree-kangaroo (Dendrolagus dorianus) is a long-tailed, furry, bear-like mammal found only in tropical mountain forests on the island of New Guinea (in Papua New Guinea)..
